worldPeriods.name: Old Kingdom Egypt
worldPeriods.note: The pyramid age — Djoser, Khufu, Khafre.

worldPeriods.name: Middle Kingdom Egypt
worldPeriods.note: Reunification after the First Intermediate Period.

worldPeriods.name: New Kingdom Egypt
worldPeriods.note: Egypt at its imperial peak — Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Ramesses II.

worldPeriods.name: Late Period & Ptolemaic Egypt
worldPeriods.note: Foreign and then Macedonian rule, ending with Cleopatra VII.

worldPeriods.name: Early Dynastic Sumer
worldPeriods.note: The first cities and the first writing, in Mesopotamia.

worldPeriods.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
worldPeriods.note: The largest empire the world had yet seen.

worldPeriods.name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
worldPeriods.note: Greece's great rival power through the Classical period.

worldPeriods.name: Roman Kingdom
worldPeriods.note: Seven legendary kings, ending with Tarquin the Proud.

worldPeriods.name: Roman Republic
worldPeriods.note: The power that eventually absorbed the entire Greek world.

worldPeriods.name: Carthage
worldPeriods.note: A Phoenician colony that grew into the western Mediterranean's dominant naval power, until Rome broke it.

worldPeriods.name: Indus Valley Civilisation
worldPeriods.note: Planned cities at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, with a still-undeciphered script.

worldPeriods.name: Vedic Civilisation
worldPeriods.note: The oral Vedas are composed; the foundations of classical Indian culture.

worldPeriods.name: Shang Dynasty China
worldPeriods.note: The first Chinese dynasty attested by contemporary writing — oracle bones.

worldPeriods.name: Zhou Dynasty China
worldPeriods.note: China's longest dynasty, spanning the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods.

worldEvents.name: Unification of Egypt
worldEvents.note: Traditional date for Narmer uniting Upper and Lower Egypt.

worldEvents.name: Great Pyramid of Giza completed
worldEvents.note: Built for Khufu — the last surviving Ancient Wonder.

worldEvents.name: Hyksos rule northern Egypt
worldEvents.note: Foreign Levantine rulers control the Nile Delta.

worldEvents.name: Hatshepsut's reign begins
worldEvents.note: One of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh in her own right.

worldEvents.name: Battle of Kadesh
worldEvents.note: Ramesses II vs. the Hittites — the earliest peace treaty to survive dates from its aftermath.

worldEvents.name: Rosetta Stone inscribed
worldEvents.note: Ptolemaic Egypt, trilingual decree — the eventual key to reading hieroglyphs.

worldEvents.name: Cleopatra VII becomes queen
worldEvents.note: The last Ptolemaic ruler, and the last pharaoh of independent Egypt.

worldEvents.name: Hammurabi's Code
worldEvents.note: One of the earliest and most complete written legal codes.

worldEvents.name: Fall of Nineveh
worldEvents.note: The Assyrian capital falls to a Babylonian-Median alliance — empire ends.

worldEvents.name: Cyrus the Great founds the Persian Empire
worldEvents.note: Conquers the Median Empire; Persia becomes the dominant power on Greece's doorstep.

worldEvents.name: Fall of Babylon to Cyrus
worldEvents.note: The Persian Empire absorbs Mesopotamia.

worldEvents.name: Founding of Rome (traditional)
worldEvents.note: The legendary date given by Roman historians themselves.

worldEvents.name: Rome becomes a Republic
worldEvents.note: The last king expelled; power passes to elected consuls.

worldEvents.name: Gauls sack Rome
worldEvents.note: A trauma Roman memory returned to for centuries.

worldEvents.name: Julius Caesar assassinated
worldEvents.note: The Republic's final crisis begins.

worldEvents.name: Augustus becomes first Roman Emperor
worldEvents.note: The Republic formally ends — three years before this dataset's own close.

worldEvents.name: Founding of Carthage (traditional)
worldEvents.note: Legendary founding by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, led by Dido.

worldEvents.name: First Punic War begins
worldEvents.note: Rome and Carthage fight for Sicily — the start of Roman naval power.

worldEvents.name: Hannibal crosses the Alps
worldEvents.note: The opening move of the Second Punic War.

worldEvents.name: Battle of Zama
worldEvents.note: Scipio defeats Hannibal — Carthage broken as a power.

worldEvents.name: Destruction of Carthage
worldEvents.note: The same year Rome also sacked Corinth — 146 BC ends Carthaginian and old Greek independence together.

worldEvents.name: Mature Harappan phase begins
worldEvents.note: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa reach their planned, standardised height.

worldEvents.name: Decline of the Indus cities
worldEvents.note: Urban centres are gradually abandoned; causes remain debated.

worldEvents.name: Shang oracle-bone script in use
worldEvents.note: The earliest confirmed form of Chinese writing, used for royal divination.

worldEvents.name: Confucius
worldEvents.note: Born during the Zhou dynasty's Spring and Autumn period; his teachings shape Chinese thought for millennia.

worldTerritories.name: Roman Empire
worldTerritories.label: Roman Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: A single schematic outline for five centuries of an empire whose real borders moved constantly (this shape leans toward its 2nd-century AD extent). Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Early Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.label: Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: The eastern Roman state after the western empire's collapse, at its broadest — including Justinian's 6th-century reconquest of Italy and the North African coast, itself temporary and unevenly held. Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Middle Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.label: Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: After the 7th-century Arab conquests stripped away Egypt, the Levant and North Africa, the empire's core settled into Anatolia and the Balkans — itself contested and shifting across five and a half centuries. Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldTerritories.name: Late Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.label: Byzantine Empire
worldTerritories.evidenceNote: After the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, the restored empire never recovered its former extent — by the 15th century it was little more than the capital and its immediate hinterland, encircled by Ottoman territory. Seed data for the known-world overview — not yet reviewed to the same standard as the Greek-world territories.

worldSites.name: Nineveh
worldSites.note: The Neo-Assyrian capital under Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal, on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul. The mounds of Kuyunjik and Nabi Yunus preserve palace and temple remains; excavation resumed in 2019 after ISIL-era destruction, and an archaeological park opened in 2023.

worldSites.name: Nimrud
worldSites.note: Ancient Kalhu, made the Assyrian imperial capital by Ashurnasirpal II. Roughly 90% of its excavated palaces and its ziggurat were destroyed by ISIL in 2015; UNESCO-backed restoration has been under way since 2017.

worldSites.name: Ashur
worldSites.note: Political capital of the Middle Assyrian kingdom and, even after the court moved elsewhere, Assyria's religious capital -- seat of the god Ashur -- until the city was destroyed in 614 BC. Temple, ziggurat and palace ruins survive on the Tigris; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003.

worldSites.name: Khorsabad (Dur-Sharrukin)
worldSites.note: A purpose-built royal city -- "Fortress of Sargon" -- constructed from scratch by Sargon II as his new capital and abandoned almost immediately after his death. Walls and gates are partly reconstructed; excavation resumed in 2023 after ISIL-era looting.

worldSites.name: Ur
worldSites.note: A Sumerian city-state, briefly the largest city in the world under the Third Dynasty of Ur (c. 2112-2004 BC). Its stepped ziggurat, dedicated to the moon god Nanna, is the best-preserved in Mesopotamia; the royal cemetery yielded the site's richest Bronze Age finds.

worldSites.name: Uruk
worldSites.note: The largest city in the world around 3100 BC, with a population estimated near 50,000, and the setting most associated with the invention of writing. The Eanna and Anu temple precincts survive as a large tell; the site remained occupied for millennia afterward.

worldSites.name: Nippur
worldSites.note: Sumer's paramount religious centre -- home to the temple of the chief god Enlil -- rather than a political capital in its own right; rulers across Mesopotamia sought legitimacy through building work here. The temple tell has been under renewed joint excavation since 2025.

worldSites.name: Susa
worldSites.note: Capital of Elam for two millennia, then one of the Achaemenid Persian Empire's four capitals alongside Persepolis, Pasargadae and Ecbatana. The Apadana palace mound and citadel survive beside modern Shush; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015.

worldSites.name: Pasargadae
worldSites.note: The first Achaemenid capital, built by Cyrus the Great after his victory over the Medes; its palace and garden complex survive, along with Cyrus's own tomb nearby. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004.

worldSites.name: Ecbatana
worldSites.note: Capital of the Median Empire, then the Achaemenid Persian kings' summer capital. The ancient mound, Hagmatana Tepe, lies mostly buried beneath modern Hamadan, which has limited excavation to occasional, small seasons.

worldSites.name: Sardis
worldSites.note: Capital of the Lydian kingdom under Gyges and Croesus, captured by Cyrus the Great in 546 BC and afterward a major Achaemenid satrapal seat. Excavations since 1958 have exposed a large gymnasium-synagogue complex, a Temple of Artemis and royal tumuli.

worldSites.name: Gordion
worldSites.note: Capital of Phrygia, associated with King Midas; its citadel mound and royal burial tumuli (including the so-called "Midas Mound") have been under active excavation since the 1950s. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

worldSites.name: Carchemish
worldSites.note: A major Hittite, then Neo-Hittite, city on the Euphrates straddling the modern Turkey-Syria border, conquered by Sargon II in 717 BC. Its citadel and lower town reopened as an archaeological park in 2019 after decades inaccessible along the border.
